claim: Proteasome inhibition elicits an evolutionarily conserved response wherein proteasome subunit mRNAs are upregulated, resulting in recovery (i.e., 'bounce-back') of proteasome activity.
source: Proteasome inhibition elicits an evolutionarily conserved response wherein proteasome subunit mRNAs are upregulated, resulting in recovery (i.e., 'bounce-back') of proteasome activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by established scientific knowledge about proteasome homeostasis and is presented as background information in the abstract.

claim: The transcription factor Nrf1/NFE2L1 mediates the proteasome bounce-back response in mammalian cells.
source: We previously demonstrated that the transcription factor Nrf1/NFE2L1 mediates this homeostatic response in mammalian cells.
evidence: This claim references prior work by the authors (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010) as indicated by the phrase 'We previously demonstrated'.

claim: Nrf1 is initially translocated into the lumen of the ER.
source: We show here that Nrf1 is initially translocated into the lumen of the ER, but is rapidly and efficiently retrotranslocated to the cytosolic side of the membrane in a manner that depends on p97/VCP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically protease protection assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Nrf1 is rapidly and efficiently retrotranslocated to the cytosolic side of the membrane in a manner that depends on p97/VCP.
source: We show here that Nrf1 is initially translocated into the lumen of the ER, but is rapidly and efficiently retrotranslocated to the cytosolic side of the membrane in a manner that depends on p97/VCP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data including p97 depletion experiments and p97 inhibitor studies shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Normally, retrotranslocated Nrf1 is degraded promptly by the proteasome and active species do not accumulate.
source: Normally, retrotranslocated Nrf1 is degraded promptly by the proteasome and active species do not accumulate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations showing that Nrf1 accumulates only when proteasomes are inhibited, as shown in Figure 1 and discussed throughout the manuscript.

claim: In cells with compromised proteasomes, retrotranslocated Nrf1 escapes degradation and is cleaved N-terminal to Leu-104 to yield a fragment that is no longer tethered to the ER membrane.
source: However, in cells with compromised proteasomes, retrotranslocated Nrf1 escapes degradation and is cleaved N-terminal to Leu-104 to yield a fragment that is no longer tethered to the ER membrane.
evidence: This claim is supported by N-terminal sequencing data (Figure 1B) and pulse-chase experiments (Figure 1D) showing cleavage at Leu-104.

claim: The cleavage event N-terminal to Leu-104 is essential for Nrf1-dependent activation of proteasome gene expression upon proteasome inhibition.
source: Importantly, this cleavage event is essential for Nrf1-dependent activation of proteasome gene expression upon proteasome inhibition.
evidence: This claim is supported by experiments with non-cleavable Nrf1 mutants showing defective PSM gene induction (Figure 2).

claim: Nrf1 belongs to the cap 'n' collar basic leucine zipper (CNC-bZIP) family of proteins that are known to be activated in response to cellular stress.
source: Transcription factor Nuclear factor erythroid derived 2-related factor 1 (Nrf1) belongs to the cap 'n' collar basic leucine zipper (CNC-bZIP) family of proteins that are known to be activated in response to cellular stress (Sykiotis and Bohmann, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sykiotis and Bohmann, 2010.

claim: Other members of the CNC-bZIP family include p45 NF-E2, Nrf2, Nrf3, Bach1, and Bach2.
source: Other members of this family include p45 NF-E2, Nrf2, Nrf3, Bach1, and Bach2 (Andrews et al., 1993; Moi et al., 1994; Oyake et al., 1996; Kobayashi et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations (Andrews et al., 1993; Moi et al., 1994; Oyake et al., 1996; Kobayashi et al., 1999).

claim: The CNC-bZIP transcription factors heterodimerize with small Maf proteins (Maf F, Maf G, and Maf K) and preferentially bind to anti-oxidant response elements (AREs) present in the promoter region of their target genes.
source: The CNC-bZIP transcriptions factors heterodimerize with small Maf proteins (Maf F, Maf G, and Maf K) and preferentially bind to anti-oxidant response elements (AREs) present in the promoter region of their target genes (Motohashi et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Motohashi et al., 2002.

claim: Nrf2 is the most studied member of the CNC-bZIP family.
source: The most studied member of the CNC-bZIP family is Nrf2, which in response to oxidative stress directs a transcriptional program that helps maintain cellular redox homeostasis (Kensler et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a statement of scientific consensus supported by citation to Kensler et al., 2007.

claim: Nrf2 directs a transcriptional program that helps maintain cellular redox homeostasis in response to oxidative stress.
source: The most studied member of the CNC-bZIP family is Nrf2, which in response to oxidative stress directs a transcriptional program that helps maintain cellular redox homeostasis (Kensler et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kensler et al., 2007.

claim: In mouse embryonic fibroblasts, Nrf1 but not Nrf2 is necessary for elevated expression of proteasome subunit mRNAs observed in cells treated with proteasome inhibitor.
source: Recently, we demonstrated that in mouse embryonic fibroblasts, Nrf1 but not Nrf2 is necessary for elevated expression of proteasome subunit mRNAs observed in cells treated with proteasome inhibitor, leading to a recovery or 'bounce-back' of proteasome activity (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim references prior work by the authors (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).

claim: TCF11 (a longer isoform of Nrf1 found only in humans) is a mediator of proteasome bounce-back response after proteasome inhibition in human cells.
source: Consistent with our observation, TCF11 (a longer isoform of Nrf1 found only in humans) was subsequently reported to be a mediator of proteasome bounce-back response after proteasome inhibition in human cells (Steffen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Steffen et al., 2010.

claim: Nrf1 functions to combat proteotoxic stress caused by proteasome inhibition in mammals akin to transcription factors RPN4 in yeast and Cnc-C in Drosophila.
source: Thus it appears that Nrf1 functions to combat proteotoxic stress caused by proteasome inhibition in mammals akin to transcription factors RPN4 in yeast (Xie and Varshavsky, 2001) and Cnc-C in Drosophila (Grimberg et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Xie and Varshavsky, 2001 and Grimberg et al., 2011, and represents an inference about functional conservation.

claim: Nrf1 depletion slows the rate of recovery of proteasome activity following transient application of a covalent proteasome inhibitor.
source: From the standpoint of cancer treatment, blockade of this bounce-back response may be a viable strategy to enhance the efficacy of proteasome inhibition therapy, given that Nrf1 depletion slows the rate of recovery of proteasome activity following transient application of a covalent proteasome inhibitor and results in enhanced proteasome inhibitor-mediated apoptosis in cancer cells (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim references prior work by the authors (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).

claim: Nrf1 depletion results in enhanced proteasome inhibitor-mediated apoptosis in cancer cells.
source: From the standpoint of cancer treatment, blockade of this bounce-back response may be a viable strategy to enhance the efficacy of proteasome inhibition therapy, given that Nrf1 depletion slows the rate of recovery of proteasome activity following transient application of a covalent proteasome inhibitor and results in enhanced proteasome inhibitor-mediated apoptosis in cancer cells (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim references prior work by the authors (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).

claim: Blockade of the Nrf1-mediated bounce-back response may be a viable strategy to enhance the efficacy of proteasome inhibition therapy.
source: From the standpoint of cancer treatment, blockade of this bounce-back response may be a viable strategy to enhance the efficacy of proteasome inhibition therapy, given that Nrf1 depletion slows the rate of recovery of proteasome activity following transient application of a covalent proteasome inhibitor and results in enhanced proteasome inhibitor-mediated apoptosis in cancer cells (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential therapeutic applications based on prior experimental data.

claim: In Nrf1−/− mouse neurons, PSM gene expression is diminished resulting in impaired proteasome function and neurodegeneration.
source: For instance, in Nrf1−/− mouse neurons, PSM gene expression is diminished resulting in impaired proteasome function and neurodegeneration (Lee et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2011.

claim: A liver-specific knockout of Nrf1 in mice caused attenuation of PSM expression in hepatocytes.
source: Also, a liver-specific knockout of Nrf1 in mice caused a similar attenuation of PSM expression in hepatocytes (Lee et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2013.

claim: Nrf1 exists in two forms, p120 and p110, both of which are unstable and accumulate when the proteasome is inhibited.
source: What is known is that Nrf1 exists in two forms, p120 and p110, both of which are unstable and accumulate when the proteasome is inhibited (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim references prior work by the authors (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).

claim: Nrf1 p120 is embedded in the ER membrane.
source: Whereas p120 is embedded in the ER membrane, p110 is soluble and can enter the nucleus (Biswas and Chan, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Biswas and Chan, 2009.

claim: Nrf1 p110 is soluble and can enter the nucleus.
source: Whereas p120 is embedded in the ER membrane, p110 is soluble and can enter the nucleus (Biswas and Chan, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Biswas and Chan, 2009.

claim: The anti-HA antibody was able to detect two different forms of Nrf1 (∼120 and ∼110 kDa) in cells expressing 3×FlagNrf1HA treated with MG132.
source: In the presence of MG132, regardless of the cell type used, we observed that although the anti-HA antibody was able to detect two different forms of Nrf1 (∼120 and ∼110 kDa), the anti-Flag antibody was able to detect only the ∼120 kDa form (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The anti-Flag antibody was able to detect only the ∼120 kDa form of Nrf1 in cells expressing 3×FlagNrf1HA treated with MG132.
source: In the presence of MG132, regardless of the cell type used, we observed that although the anti-HA antibody was able to detect two different forms of Nrf1 (∼120 and ∼110 kDa), the anti-Flag antibody was able to detect only the ∼120 kDa form (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Nrf1 p120 is cleaved somewhere close to the N-terminus to yield p110.
source: The simplest explanation for this observation is that Nrf1 p120 was cleaved somewhere close to the N-terminus to yield p110.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential detection of Nrf1 forms by N-terminal vs C-terminal tags.

claim: The p110 form of Nrf1 has a new N-terminus starting with Leu-104.
source: Although the ∼120 kDa band confirmed the intact N-terminus of the full-length Nrf1, sequence from the ∼110 kDa band was consistent with a new N-terminus starting with Leu-104 (Figure 1B; putative cleavage site indicated with a scissor).
evidence: This claim is supported by N-terminal Edman degradation sequencing data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: All mutants (m1 through m6) flanking the predicted cleavage site were defective to varying degrees in their ability to be processed to the p110 form.
source: We found that all mutants were defective to varying degrees in their ability to be processed to the p110 form, although the defects of m4 and m6 were relatively modest (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Trp-103 at the P1 position plays a crucial role for protease recognition in Nrf1 processing.
source: Interestingly, m4 and m6 are the only mutants that retain Trp-103 at the P1 position (with respect to the cleavage site), implying a crucial role of this Trp residue for protease recognition.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that mutants retaining Trp-103 showed less severe processing defects.

claim: Wild-type p120 Nrf1 is processed to p110 over time in a pulse-chase experiment.
source: We observed that over time, wild-type p120 was processed to p110 but the non-cleavable Nrf1(m1)3×Flag was not processed (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulse-chase experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The non-cleavable Nrf1(m1)3×Flag mutant is not processed to p110 in a pulse-chase experiment.
source: We observed that over time, wild-type p120 was processed to p110 but the non-cleavable Nrf1(m1)3×Flag was not processed (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulse-chase experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Newly synthesized Nrf1 p120 undergoes proteolytic processing between Trp-103 and Leu-104 to generate the p110 form.
source: Taken together, our data are consistent with a model in which newly synthesized Nrf1 p120 undergoes proteolytic processing between Trp-103 and Leu-104 to generate the p110 form.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple lines of experimental evidence including sequencing and mutagenesis data.

claim: Wild-type Nrf13×Flag is able to reinstate the induction of proteasome subunit (PSM) genes in response to MG132 treatment in Nrf1−/− MEFs.
source: As expected, wild-type Nrf13×Flag was able to reinstate the induction of proteasome subunit (PSM) genes in response to MG132 treatment in these cells (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Non-cleavable Nrf1(m1)3×Flag is defective in inducing PSM genes upon MG132 treatment in Nrf1−/− MEFs.
source: In contrast, non-cleavable Nrf1(m1)3×Flag was defective in inducing PSM genes under the same conditions, implicating a necessary role for proteolytic processing in Nrf1's transcriptional program.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Proteolytic processing plays a necessary role in Nrf1's transcriptional program.
source: In contrast, non-cleavable Nrf1(m1)3×Flag was defective in inducing PSM genes under the same conditions, implicating a necessary role for proteolytic processing in Nrf1's transcriptional program.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that non-cleavable Nrf1 mutants fail to induce PSM genes.

claim: p97 is a homo-hexameric AAA ATPase that is implicated in numerous cellular processes ranging from cell-cycle regulation to membrane fusion and protein degradation.
source: p97 is a homo-hexameric AAA ATPase that is implicated in numerous cellular processes ranging from cell-cycle regulation to membrane fusion and protein degradation (Ye, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ye, 2006 and represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: p97 has been implicated in the turnover of the TCF11 isoform of human Nrf1 via the endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) pathway.
source: p97 has also been implicated in the turnover of the TCF11 isoform of human Nrf1 via the endoplasmic reticulum-associated degradation (ERAD) pathway (Steffen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Steffen et al., 2010.

claim: Depletion of p97 leads to the strong accumulation of ubiquitin-conjugated substrates.
source: Similar to inhibition of the proteasome, depletion of p97 leads to the strong accumulation of ubiquitin-conjugated substrates (Wojcik et al., 2004), underscoring its role in enabling degradation of a subset of the ubiquitinated proteome by the proteasome (Kolawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Wojcik et al., 2004 and Kolawa et al., 2013.

claim: p97 plays a role in enabling degradation of a subset of the ubiquitinated proteome by the proteasome.
source: Similar to inhibition of the proteasome, depletion of p97 leads to the strong accumulation of ubiquitin-conjugated substrates (Wojcik et al., 2004), underscoring its role in enabling degradation of a subset of the ubiquitinated proteome by the proteasome (Kolawa et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kolawa et al., 2013.

claim: Depletion of p97 does not induce the bounce-back response in NIH-3T3 mouse fibroblasts.
source: Unlike proteasome inhibition, depletion of p97 upon addition of doxycycline did not induce the bounce-back response (Figure 3A; compare bars 1 and 3 for the PSM genes).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: MG132-mediated bounce-back response is severely impaired when p97 is knocked-down.
source: By contrast, we observed that MG132-mediated bounce-back response was severely impaired when p97 was knocked-down (Figure 3A; compare bars 3 and 4 for the PSM genes).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative RT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Nrf1 accumulates in cells depleted of p97.
source: Consistent with Steffen et al., 2010, Nrf1 accumulated in cells depleted of p97 (Figure 3B, compare lanes 1 and 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B and is consistent with prior literature.

claim: Control cells treated with MG132 accumulate the p110 form of Nrf1.
source: Whereas the control cells accumulated p110 (indicative of Nrf1 activation), this form was markedly absent in p97-depleted cells (Figure 3B, compare lanes 2 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The p110 form of Nrf1 is markedly absent in p97-depleted cells treated with MG132.
source: Whereas the control cells accumulated p110 (indicative of Nrf1 activation), this form was markedly absent in p97-depleted cells (Figure 3B, compare lanes 2 and 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Treatment of NIH-3T3 mouse fibroblasts with NMS-873 leads to a robust accumulation of p120 Nrf1.
source: Treatment of NIH-3T3 mouse fibroblasts or HEK-293-Nrf13×Flag cells with NMS-873 led to a robust accumulation of p120 Nrf1 (Figure 3C; lane 1), which was then efficiently converted to the p110 form with a half-life of ∼30 min upon washout of NMS-873 in the presence of cycloheximide and MG132 (Figure 3C, lanes 2–6).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulse-chase experimental data with p97 inhibitor shown in Figure 3C.

claim: p120 Nrf1 is efficiently converted to the p110 form with a half-life of ∼30 min upon washout of NMS-873 in the presence of cycloheximide and MG132.
source: Treatment of NIH-3T3 mouse fibroblasts or HEK-293-Nrf13×Flag cells with NMS-873 led to a robust accumulation of p120 Nrf1 (Figure 3C; lane 1), which was then efficiently converted to the p110 form with a half-life of ∼30 min upon washout of NMS-873 in the presence of cycloheximide and MG132 (Figure 3C, lanes 2–6).
evidence: This claim is supported by pulse-chase experimental data with p97 inhibitor shown in Figure 3C.

claim: p97 controls not only the degradation of Nrf1, but also its processing to the active p110 form.
source: Thus, our results are consistent with a model in which p97 controls not only the degradation of Nrf1, but also its processing to the active p110 form.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental observations including p97 depletion and inhibitor studies.

claim: During synthesis, Nrf1 becomes anchored in the ER membrane via an N-terminal transmembrane region (residues 7–24).
source: It has been proposed that during synthesis, Nrf1 becomes anchored in the ER membrane via an N-terminal transmembrane region (residues 7–24) (Zhang and Hayes, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhang and Hayes, 2010.

claim: The N-terminus of 3×FlagNrf1 is oriented towards the cytosol regardless of p97 status.
source: Regardless of p97 status (normal in the absence of doxycycline, or depleted in the presence of doxycycline, Figure 4A), 3×FlagNrf1 was susceptible to Proteinase K (PK) digestion in the absence of detergent, implying that the N-terminus was oriented towards the cytosol at all times.
evidence: This claim is supported by protease protection assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The orientation of the C-terminus of Nrf13×Flag shows a strong dependence on p97 status.
source: Interestingly, however, the orientation of the C-terminus of Nrf13×Flag showed a strong dependence on p97 status (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by protease protection assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In mock-depleted cells, Nrf13×Flag is largely susceptible to digestion by Proteinase K.
source: In mock-depleted cells, Nrf13×Flag was largely susceptible to digestion by PK (Figure 4B, compare lanes 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by protease protection assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: When p97 is depleted, Nrf13×Flag is largely resistant to Proteinase K.
source: In stark contrast, when p97 was depleted by the addition of doxycycline, Nrf13×Flag was largely resistant to PK (Figure 4B, compare lanes 7 and 8, or lanes 10 and 11).
evidence: This claim is supported by protease protection assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Only a very small amino-terminal segment of newly-synthesized Nrf1 (amino acids 1–6) is exposed to the cytosol, whereas the bulk of Nrf1 (amino acids 25–742) remains in the lumen of the ER when the retrotranslocation activity of p97 is blocked.
source: The different behaviors of 3×FlagNrf1 and Nrf13×Flag and the failure to observe detectable trimming of Nrf13×Flag are consistent with a topology wherein only a very small amino-terminal segment of newly-synthesized Nrf1 is exposed to the cytosol (amino acids 1–6), whereas the bulk of Nrf1 (amino acids 25–742) remains in the lumen of the ER when the retrotranslocation activity of p97 is blocked.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential protease sensitivity of N-terminally vs C-terminally tagged Nrf1.

claim: Retrotranslocation of p120 Nrf1 constitutively occurs at such a fast rate that, at steady-state, only a tiny fraction of luminal p120 can be detected unless retrotranslocation is blocked by depletion of p97.
source: We propose that retrotranslocation of p120 constitutively occurs at such a fast rate that, at steady-state, only a tiny fraction of luminal p120 can be detected unless retrotranslocation is blocked by depletion of p97 as in Figure 4B.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on the observation of a small protease-resistant pool of p120 at steady-state.

claim: Nrf13×Flag becomes sensitive to Proteinase K upon washout of NMS-873 in the presence of MG132 plus cycloheximide.
source: Whereas Nrf13×Flag was largely resistant to digestion by PK in HEK293 cells treated with NMS-873 (Figure 4D, lanes 1 and 2), it became sensitive to PK upon washout of NMS-873 in the presence of MG132 plus cycloheximide (Figure 4D, lanes 4 and 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by protease protection assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Nrf1(m1)3×Flag mirrors the behavior of wild-type Nrf1 in protease protection assays.
source: Nrf1(m1)3×Flag mirrored the behavior of the wild-type protein (Figure 4D), indicating that the lack of processing observed for non-cleavable mutant was not due to defective retrotranslocation.
evidence: This claim is supported by protease protection assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The lack of processing observed for non-cleavable Nrf1 mutant is not due to defective retrotranslocation.
source: Nrf1(m1)3×Flag mirrored the behavior of the wild-type protein (Figure 4D), indicating that the lack of processing observed for non-cleavable mutant was not due to defective retrotranslocation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that non-cleavable Nrf1 undergoes retrotranslocation normally.

claim: When the C-terminal domain (CTD) of Nrf1 is oriented towards the lumen, Nrf1 should be glycosylated on a set of Asn-X-Ser/Thr sites C-terminal to the transmembrane domain.
source: We reasoned that when the C-terminal domain (CTD) is oriented towards the lumen, Nrf1 should be glycosylated on a set of Asn-X-Ser/Thr sites C-terminal to the transmembrane domain (Zhang et al., 2007), whereas when the CTD is retrotranslocated to the cytosol, it should become degylcosylated.
evidence: This is a prediction based on established knowledge about N-linked glycosylation in the ER lumen, supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2007.

claim: When the CTD of Nrf1 is retrotranslocated to the cytosol, it should become deglycosylated.
source: We reasoned that when the C-terminal domain (CTD) is oriented towards the lumen, Nrf1 should be glycosylated on a set of Asn-X-Ser/Thr sites C-terminal to the transmembrane domain (Zhang et al., 2007), whereas when the CTD is retrotranslocated to the cytosol, it should become degylcosylated.
evidence: This is a prediction based on established knowledge about protein glycosylation and the cytosolic environment.

claim: Nrf1 p120 that accumulated in cells treated with NMS-873 is sensitive to Endoglycosidase H.
source: Nrf1 p120 that accumulated in cells treated with NMS-873 was sensitive to Endo H (Figure 4E, compare lanes 1 and 2 or 5 and 6), whereas it became largely resistant to Endo H upon being chased in the presence of MG132 plus cycloheximide (Figure 4E, compare lanes 3 and 4 or 7 and 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by deglycosylation assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Nrf1 p120 becomes largely resistant to Endoglycosidase H upon being chased in the presence of MG132 plus cycloheximide after NMS-873 washout.
source: Nrf1 p120 that accumulated in cells treated with NMS-873 was sensitive to Endo H (Figure 4E, compare lanes 1 and 2 or 5 and 6), whereas it became largely resistant to Endo H upon being chased in the presence of MG132 plus cycloheximide (Figure 4E, compare lanes 3 and 4 or 7 and 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by deglycosylation assay data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The CTD of p120 Nrf1 flips from a luminal to a cytosolic orientation upon restoration of p97 activity.
source: This behavior is consistent with the protease protection data that indicated that the CTD of p120 flips from a luminal to a cytosolic orientation upon restoration of p97 activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on both protease protection and glycosylation data.

claim: Once retrotranslocated to the cytosol, Nrf1 is not only deglycosylated and proteolytically cleaved after Trp103, but it also gains one or more additional modifications, the nature of which remains unknown.
source: Our data suggest that once it is retrotranslocated to the cytosol, Nrf1 is not only deglycosylated and proteolytically cleaved after Trp103, but it also gains one or more additional modifications, the nature of which remains unknown.
evidence: This is an inference based on the unexpectedly slow migration of processed Nrf1 on SDS-PAGE compared to unmodified protein.

claim: Mouse Nrf1 and its human ortholog TCF11 are transcription factors that enhance the accumulation of mRNAs that encode proteasome subunits upon inhibition of proteasome activity.
source: Mouse Nrf1 and its human ortholog TCF11 are transcription factors that enhance the accumulation of mRNAs that encode proteasome subunits upon inhibition of proteasome activity (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010; Steffen et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Radhakrishnan et al., 2010 and Steffen et al., 2010.

claim: Nrf1 is initially integrated into the ER membrane but is turned over rapidly.
source: Prior work established that Nrf1 is initially integrated into the ER membrane but is turned over rapidly (Biswas and Chan, 2009; Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Biswas and Chan, 2009 and Radhakrishnan et al., 2010.

claim: Upon proteasome inhibition, Nrf1 accumulates, migrates to the nucleus, and activates gene expression.
source: Upon proteasome inhibition, it accumulates, migrates to the nucleus, and activates gene expression.
evidence: This is a summary of established findings from prior work.

claim: The domains of Nrf1 that are implicated in transcriptional activation are initially translocated into the lumen of the ER.
source: Specifically, we show that the domains of Nrf1 that are implicated in transcriptional activation are initially translocated into the lumen of the ER, but subsequently are retrotranslocated to the cytosolic side of the membrane in a manner that depends on the AAA ATPase p97/VCP.
evidence: This claim is supported by protease protection and glycosylation data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The domains of Nrf1 that are implicated in transcriptional activation are subsequently retrotranslocated to the cytosolic side of the membrane in a manner that depends on the AAA ATPase p97/VCP.
source: Specifically, we show that the domains of Nrf1 that are implicated in transcriptional activation are initially translocated into the lumen of the ER, but subsequently are retrotranslocated to the cytosolic side of the membrane in a manner that depends on the AAA ATPase p97/VCP.
evidence: This claim is supported by p97 depletion and inhibitor experiments shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: In unperturbed cells, retrotranslocated Nrf1 is promptly degraded by the proteasome, resulting in a futile cycle of continuous synthesis, membrane insertion, retrotranslocation, and degradation.
source: In unperturbed cells, the retrotranslocated Nrf1 is promptly degraded by the proteasome, resulting in a futile cycle of continuous synthesis, membrane insertion, retrotranslocation, and degradation (Figure 5, left-hand side).
evidence: This is a model based on the integration of multiple experimental observations and is depicted in Figure 5.

claim: In cells with compromised proteasome activity, some of the retrotranslocated Nrf1 escapes degradation and is cleaved on the N-terminal side of Leu-104 to yield a p110 fragment that is no longer tethered to the ER membrane and can migrate to the nucleus.
source: However, in cells with compromised proteasome activity, some of the retrotranslocated Nrf1 escapes degradation and is cleaved on the N-terminal side of Leu-104 to yield a p110 fragment that is no longer tethered to the ER membrane and can migrate to the nucleus (Figure 5, right-hand side).
evidence: This is a model based on the integration of multiple experimental observations and is depicted in Figure 5.

claim: Cleavage by the site-1 and site-2 proteases involved in mobilization of SREBP appears unlikely to be responsible for Nrf1 processing.
source: Cleavage by the site-1 and site-2 proteases involved in mobilization of SREBP appears unlikely, because CHO cell lines deficient in these activities (Rawson et al., 1997, 1998) were nonetheless able to accumulate p110 upon proteasome inhibition (R Rawson, personal communication).
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished data from a personal communication and citations to Rawson et al., 1997, 1998.

claim: The proteasome appears to be dispensable for cleavage of Nrf1 p120 to p110.
source: In addition, the proteasome, which cleaves Spt23 and Mga2 from the ER membrane in yeast (Hoppe et al., 2000), appears to be dispensable for cleavage because we observed robust formation of p110 in two different cell lines with three different proteasome inhibitors across a wide range of concentrations (Figure 1, and data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations with proteasome inhibitors and citation to Hoppe et al., 2000.

claim: An inhibitor of ER-localized rhomboid protease(s) failed to impede the accumulation of p110 in cells treated with MG132.
source: Finally, an inhibitor of ER-localized rhomboid protease(s) (Pierrat et al., 2011) failed to impede the accumulation of p110 in cells treated with MG132 (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on unpublished experimental data and citation to Pierrat et al., 2011.

claim: In unperturbed cells, p97-dependent retrotranslocation and proteasome-dependent degradation are so intimately coupled that there is no opportunity for the cleavage event to occur as Nrf1 is threaded from the membrane into the maw of the proteasome.
source: Although it will be easier to address this question when the protease is in hand, a reasonable working hypothesis is that in unperturbed cells, p97-dependent retrotranslocation and proteasome-dependent degradation are so intimately coupled that there is no opportunity for the cleavage event to occur as Nrf1 is threaded from the membrane into the maw of the proteasome.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed to explain why p110 does not accumulate in unperturbed cells.

claim: When the proteasome is inhibited, Nrf1 accumulates on the cytosolic side of the membrane where it is susceptible to cleavage.
source: However, when the proteasome is inhibited, Nrf1 accumulates on the cytosolic side of the membrane where it is susceptible to cleavage.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that p110 accumulates when proteasomes are inhibited.

claim: p110 is intrinsically unstable.
source: Even if the protease occasionally intercedes before the proteasome can act and small amounts of p110 are generated, p110 is intrinsically unstable (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010) and thus does not accumulate to substantial levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Radhakrishnan et al., 2010.

claim: The activation of Nrf1 differs markedly from the activation of all other ER membrane-tethered transcription factors that have been studied to date, including SREBP, ATF6, OASIS, CREB-H, Spt23, and Mga2.
source: It should be immediately evident from the foregoing discussion how the activation of Nrf1 differs markedly from the activation of all other ER membrane-tethered transcription factors that have been studied to date, including SREBP, ATF6, OASIS, CREB-H, Spt23, and Mga2 (Brown and Goldstein, 1997; Hoppe et al., 2000; Ye et al., 2000; Kondo et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a comparative analysis based on the novel findings about Nrf1 and established knowledge about other ER membrane-tethered transcription factors, supported by multiple citations.

claim: For SREBP, ATF6, OASIS, CREB-H, Spt23, and Mga2, the precursor is inserted into the ER membrane such that the functional domains involved in transcription are displayed on the cytosolic side of the membrane.
source: In all of those cases, the precursor is inserted into the ER membrane such that the functional domains involved in transcription are displayed on the cytosolic side of the membrane.
evidence: This is established knowledge about other ER membrane-tethered transcription factors.

claim: For SREBP, ATF6, OASIS, CREB-H, Spt23, and Mga2, cleavages in the cytosolic or intramembrane domains can liberate soluble fragments that translocate to the nucleus.
source: Cleavages in the cytosolic or intramembrane domains can therefore liberate soluble fragments that translocate to the nucleus.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the activation mechanism of other ER membrane-tethered transcription factors.

claim: Since Nrf1 begins its life with its functional domains in the ER lumen, it must be retrotranslocated to the cytosol before processing can yield a functional fragment that can relocalize to the nucleus.
source: By contrast, since Nrf1 begins its life with its functional domains in the ER lumen, it must be retrotranslocated to the cytosol before processing can yield a functional fragment that can relocalize to the nucleus.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the experimental findings about Nrf1 topology and processing.

claim: The p97-dependent retrotranslocation pathway traversed by Nrf1 is normally employed to clear misfolded proteins from the ER.
source: However, because the p97-dependent retrotranslocation pathway traversed by Nrf1 is normally employed to clear misfolded proteins from the ER (Wolf and Stolz, 2012), the inevitable consequence of Nrf1 piggybacking on this mechanism is that it is rapidly degraded by the proteasome as soon as it gains access to the cytosol.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wolf and Stolz, 2012 and represents established knowledge about ERAD.

claim: The inevitable consequence of Nrf1 piggybacking on the p97-dependent retrotranslocation mechanism is that it is rapidly degraded by the proteasome as soon as it gains access to the cytosol.
source: However, because the p97-dependent retrotranslocation pathway traversed by Nrf1 is normally employed to clear misfolded proteins from the ER (Wolf and Stolz, 2012), the inevitable consequence of Nrf1 piggybacking on this mechanism is that it is rapidly degraded by the proteasome as soon as it gains access to the cytosol.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of the ERAD pathway and the experimental observations about Nrf1.

claim: The coupling of retrotranslocation to degradation precludes the accumulation of Nrf1 precursor on the cytosolic side of the ER membrane, except under circumstances where there is insufficient proteasome activity to keep pace with the appearance of substrates.
source: This precludes the accumulation of Nrf1 precursor on the cytosolic side of the ER membrane, except under circumstances where there is insufficient proteasome activity to keep pace with the appearance of substrates.
evidence: This is an inference that explains the conditional activation of Nrf1 based on the experimental observations.

claim: Ricin is retrotranslocated from the ER lumen to the cytosol, where it exerts its biological function.
source: Ricin, a plant toxin, and some bacterial toxins including cholera toxin, and shiga toxin likewise are retrotranslocated from the ER lumen to the cytosol, where they exert their biological functions (Inoue et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Inoue et al., 2011.

claim: Cholera toxin and shiga toxin are retrotranslocated from the ER lumen to the cytosol, where they exert their biological functions.
source: Ricin, a plant toxin, and some bacterial toxins including cholera toxin, and shiga toxin likewise are retrotranslocated from the ER lumen to the cytosol, where they exert their biological functions (Inoue et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Inoue et al., 2011.

claim: The Hepatitis E Virus capsid protein ORF2 co-opts the ERAD machinery to gain access to the cytosol.
source: Another example is the Hepatitis E Virus capsid protein ORF2, which co-opts the ERAD machinery to gain access to the cytosol (Surjit et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Surjit et al., 2007.

claim: Calreticulin is the only known host protein that undergoes retrotranslocation from the ER but escapes degradation by the proteasome.
source: To our knowledge, the only host protein that undergoes retrotranslocation from the ER but escapes degradation by the proteasome is calreticulin (Afshar et al., 2005; Gold et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Afshar et al., 2005 and Gold et al., 2010.

claim: Upon inhibition of the proteasome, presumably the entire complement of ERAD substrates mimics Nrf1 in that these proteins are retrotranslocated from the luminal to the cytosolic side of the ER membrane but are not degraded.
source: Upon inhibition of the proteasome, presumably the entire complement of ERAD substrates mimics Nrf1 in that these proteins are retrotranslocated from the luminal to the cytosolic side of the ER membrane but are not degraded.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the general mechanism of ERAD and proteasome inhibition.

claim: Targeting Nrf1 to the ER may ensure that the basal level of Nrf1 activity is essentially zero in the absence of proteasome stress, due to the normally tight coupling between retrotranslocation and degradation.
source: Targeting Nrf1 to the ER may ensure that the basal level of Nrf1 activity is essentially zero in the absence of proteasome stress, due to the normally tight coupling between retrotranslocation and degradation (Wolf and Stolz, 2012).
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the biological rationale of Nrf1's unusual activation mechanism, supported by citation to Wolf and Stolz, 2012.

claim: In cells that experience insufficient proteasome activity, accumulation of active Nrf1 can restore an adequate level of proteasome function.
source: In cells that experience insufficient proteasome activity—brought about either through environmental insults including proteasome or chaperone inhibitors produced by microbes, or through changes in gene expression—accumulation of active Nrf1 can restore an adequate level of proteasome function.
evidence: This is an inference about the biological function of the Nrf1 activation mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: In cancer cells, depletion of Nrf1 slows down recovery of proteasome activity upon transient inhibition of the proteasome and enhances apoptosis caused by a covalent proteasome inhibitor.
source: Previously, we demonstrated that in cancer cells, depletion of Nrf1 slows down recovery of proteasome activity upon transient inhibition of the proteasome and enhances apoptosis caused by a covalent proteasome inhibitor (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim references prior work by the authors (Radhakrishnan et al., 2010).

claim: p97 is a druggable target.
source: Although inhibition of transcription factors with small molecules has proven difficult (Berg, 2008), p97 is a druggable target (Chou et al., 2011, 2013; Magnaghi et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Berg, 2008; Chou et al., 2011, 2013; and Magnaghi et al., 2013.

claim: Recent papers have reported enhanced killing of cancer cells when proteasome and p97 inhibitors are used in combination.
source: Indeed, recent papers have reported enhanced killing of cancer cells when proteasome and p97 inhibitors are used in combination (Auner et al., 2013; Chou et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Auner et al., 2013 and Chou et al., 2013.

claim: Blockade of the Nrf1-mediated bounce-back response through inhibition of p97 may enhance the efficacy of proteasome inhibitor therapy in multiple myeloma or enable expansion of proteasome inhibitor therapy into new indications.
source: It will be interesting to see whether blockade of the Nrf1-mediated bounce-back response through inhibition of p97 enhances the efficacy of proteasome inhibitor therapy in multiple myeloma or enables expansion of proteasome inhibitor therapy into new indications.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: NMS-873 is a reversible inhibitor of p97.
source: To address this possibility, we made use of the recently described compound NMS-873, a reversible inhibitor of p97 (Magnaghi et al., 2013; Polucci et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Magnaghi et al., 2013 and Polucci et al., 2013.
